title: A gene that kills in pairs
hook: A gene kills animals that get two copies. What does selection do with it in the long run?

knows: each individual carries two copies of a gene
natural selection favours variants that help survival
doesNotKnow: that selection can hold a harmful allele at a stable share
that this happens when carrying one copy beats carrying none

misconception: Selection always removes a harmful allele.
objective: The learner can explain that when one copy of w helps (100% vs 85% survival) and two copies kill, w rises when rare and falls when common, settling where the two balance: 0.15/1.15, about 13% of copies.

claims.text: With survival AA = 1 - s, Aw = 1 and ww = 1 - t, selection holds w at a stable share q = s/(s + t); with s = 0.15 and t = 1 that is 0.15/(0.15 + 1) = 15/115, about 13% of gene copies. The stage shows the balance line and value only once the curves reach generation 60.
claims.source: Hartl D.L. & Clark A.G. (2007) Principles of Population Genetics, 4th ed., ch. 5 (overdominance). 0.15/1.15 = 0.1304, recomputed in node (artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs).

claims.text: On the stage, starting from 1% w and from 50% w, the share of w reaches about 13% by generation 60 and stays there. With no-copy survival at 95% the balance is 5% (the 1% start has only reached about 4% by generation 60); at 70% the balance is 23%.
claims.source: Deterministic recursion q' = pq / (p^2(1-s) + 2pq) (artifacts/scratch/w2life/check.mjs; fact-check 2026-10-13): from 0.01, 13.0% at gen 50; from 0.5, 13.0% at gen 50; at 95% survival the 1% start is 4.1% at gen 60 and the equilibrium 4.76%; 70% gives 23.1%. No random seed.

claims.text: When w is rare almost no young get two copies while some get one and survive best, so w rises; when w is common a large share of young get two copies and die, so w falls. On the stage the young with two copies are q^2 of the young and those with one copy 2pq (1% w: about 0% and 2%; 50% w: 25% and 50%).
claims.source: Rare w: almost all w copies are in Aw (fitness 1 > mean fitness), so q rises; common w: the ww share q^2 grows, mean fitness of w copies falls below the mean (Hartl & Clark 2007 ch. 5).

claims.text: A real example of this balance is the sickle-cell haemoglobin allele where malaria is common: one copy protects against severe malaria; its numbers differ from the lesson's.
claims.source: Allison A.C. (1954) Br. Med. J. 1:290-294; Aidoo M. et al. (2002) Lancet 359:1311-1312.

claims.text: The species and survival numbers are made up; the model assumes random mating and a very large population (no drift).
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx, stated on the stage before the prediction (survival numbers) and in the reveal.

claims.text: The lower the survival of animals with no w, the bigger the edge of carrying one copy, and the higher the balance: s/(s + 1) is 5% at 95% survival, 13% at 85%, 23% at 70%.
claims.source: q* = s/(s + t) with t = 1 and s = 1 - survival with no w (as c1).

recall.question: An allele kills in two copies but gives carriers of one copy an edge. Over many generations, selection usually…
options: keeps it at a steady share
recall.why: Rare, it is mostly in carriers who do best, so it rises; common, more two-copy young die, so it falls. It settles in between.
